workEn: The Secret History of the Mongols
title: 元朝秘史 §§149–150
titleEn: The Secret History of the Mongols — §§149–150: Tarqutai Seized and Let Go, and the Kereid Come In
part: §§149–150 — Tarqutai Seized and Let Go, and the Kereid Come In
source: Mongγol-un niγuča tobčiyan (The Secret History of the Mongols), §§149–150, in the Ming Chinese-character phonetic transcription, as edited with a romanized reading by Shiratori Kurakichi 白鳥庫吉, 音訳蒙文元朝秘史 (Tokyo, 1943), itself based on the Ye Dehui 葉德輝 printed edition of 1905/1908; text taken from the Japanese Wikisource transcription, archived and verified against it character for character. Shiratori died in 1942, so the edition was public domain in Japan before the URAA date and was never restored in the United States. Section numbering (§) is the standard citation system. Romanization convention: Shiratori's, kept exactly as he prints it (γ, ġ, ṅ, ž, č, and the raised dot of γ̇). Translations are made fresh from the Mongolian, with the Ming interlinear Chinese glosses as the primary crib. No modern translation was consulted. langCode is null: there is no text-to-speech for Middle Mongol.
about: Two sections. §149: the old man Shirgügetü and his sons, who bear a grudge against the Taichi'ud noyan Tarqutai-Kiriltuq, seize him and put him on a cart; Tarqutai's own sons and brothers give chase, and Shirgügetü, astride him with a knife, is about to cut his throat when Tarqutai himself calls them off, saying he knows Temüjin as a boy, whom he could never bring himself to have killed. Shirgügetü's sons then take Naya'a's counsel, free Tarqutai at Qutuqul-Nu'u, and come to Chinggis Qahan, who commends their loyalty to their own lord. §150: Jaqagambu and many scattered Kereid come over to Chinggis, and the text goes back to explain the bond between Wang Qahan of the Kereid and Yesügei Qahan; the part ends in the middle of that sentence. The passage of the knife (Shirgügetü's speech and Tarqutai's reply) and the double reasoning of Naya'a rest heavily on the Ming glosses, and several clauses are first readings, as the notes say.
draftNote: The Mongol readings follow Shiratori throughout; the English is a first drafting.

sentences.l: Ničügüd-Baγ̇arin's Širġüġetü old man, Alaγ, Najaγ̇a, sons-with-his-own, Taičiγ̇ud's noyan Tarqutai-Kiriltuγ forest-entering being-ACC, grudge-having men were.
sentences.i: The old man Shirgügetü of the Nichügüd-Ba'arin, with his sons Alaq and Naya'a, were men with a grudge against Tarqutai-Kiriltuq, the Taichi'ud noyan, who had taken to the forest.
sentences.n: Read this as one long sentence with its verb at the end: the subject is the old man with his sons (köġüd-lüġe-ben, 'together with his own sons': plural -d, comitative -lüġe, reflexive-possessive -ben); the object is the noyan Tarqutai-Kiriltuq, who is 'forest-entering' (hoilažu, Ming 入林着, 'taking to the woods') and 'being' (büküi) with the accusative -ji (Ming 行, which marks the object here); the predicate is 'grudge-having men' (öštü, -tü as in the possessive pattern: 'one who has an enmity'). That Alaq and Naya'a are themselves sons rests on a later unit ('Alaq, Naya'a and the others, the sons of the old man Shirgügetü'); köġüd-lüġe-ben may also cover further sons, and the Ming 兒子每 stands on köġüd, not on the names. Alaγ is a name here (Ming 人名), though the same letters mean 'mottled' elsewhere. Tarqutai appears as Tarqutai-Kiriltuγ and as Tarqutai alone; I take it as one man with a by-name.

The subject is the old man and his sons.

sentences.l: Tarqutai-Kiriltuγ's sons, younger-brothers, his, snatching 'let-us-take' saying, chasing came-is.
sentences.i: Tarqutai-Kiriltuq's sons and younger brothers came chasing after them, saying, 'Let us snatch him away.'
sentences.n: Now the other side: Tarqutai's sons and younger brothers (deġü-ner: deġü 'younger brother' plus the plural -ner). buližu abuja keġen is 'snatching, let-us-take, saying': abuja is ab- 'to take' plus -ja, 'let us' (the Ming 咱 'we/us'). irežüġüi is ire- 'to come' with the narrative past -žüġüi (the same ending the earlier parts read in irežüġüi; Ming 來了 'came'). In-ü is the genitive of the third-person pronoun, 'his', and I take it to point back to Tarqutai.

sentences.t: Köġüd deġü-ner-i in-ü güjičežü ireküi-lüġe

morph.gloss: accusative or dative (Ming 行); unexplained here [行]
his, her (genitive of the 3rd-person pronoun, written in-ü) [他的]

sentences.l: The sons, younger-brothers-ACC, his, chasing, with-coming,
sentences.i: As those sons and brothers of his came up in pursuit,
sentences.n: Read this as the same pursuit, restated: the sons (Köġüd), the younger brothers, 'his' chasing, 'with the coming' (ireküi-lüġe: the comitative -lüġe on a participle, 'as, the moment that', Ming 時). The -i on deġü-ner-i is the puzzle: the Ming gives 行, the accusative or dative, which would make the brothers the objects of the chase, yet the sense needs them as the chasers. I follow the sense and mark the -i as unexplained.

sentences.t: Širġüġetü ebügen bosun jadaqu Tarqutai-ji tergen deġere unužu

morph.gloss: accusative: marks the object (after a vowel)

sentences.l: Širġüġetü old man, rising unable Tarqutai-ACC, cart upon, mounting,
sentences.i: the old man Shirgügetü climbed up on the cart, where Tarqutai, who could not get up, was lying,
sentences.n: Shirgügetü is the subject of unužu 'mounting'; Tarqutai, 'unable to rise' (bosun jadaqu: bosu- 'to rise' plus the converb -n, then jada- 'to be unable' plus the participle -qu, Ming 起不能的), is the object. Whether Tarqutai was bound or ill the text does not say. I read the accusative as 'on the cart, (him) lying', hence the added 'where Tarqutai was lying'; the next unit supplies the lying (gedergü).

sentences.l: Lying-back above, his astride sitting, knife drawing-out, speaking:
sentences.i: and, with Tarqutai lying on his back beneath him, he sat astride him, drew a knife, and said:
sentences.n: gedergü (Ming 偃仰 'leaning back, supine') I take as 'lying on the back', a word I cannot analyse further; deġere 'above' then means he sat on top. aγtalan saγužu is 'riding-astride sitting' (aγta 'gelding', -la- 'to ride', so 'sitting astride'). γarγažu: γar- 'to go out' with the causative -γa-, 'making go out', so 'drawing' the knife. The colon closes at ügülerün 'when speaking'; the quotation opens in the next unit and Shirgügetü speaks through the unit ending üküšü.

sentences.l: Son, younger-brothers your you-ACC snatching, taking-to, came.
sentences.i: 'Your sons and brothers have come to snatch you away and carry you off.'
sentences.n: The speaker is Shirgügetü, to Tarqutai. Köġün is singular in form and in the Ming (兒子); with deġü-ner and čin-u 'your' I take 'your son and younger brothers' (the sons of the earlier pursuit) as the joint subject of irebe. A vocative 'boy' is possible in the abstract, but nothing marks it and Shirgügetü calls Tarqutai 'my own lord' in the next breath. čin-u and čima-ji are the genitive and accusative of či 'you'; abura is ab- 'to take' with -ra, which I gloss 'in order to' (buližu abura irebe, 'came to snatch and take').

sentences.l: You-ACC, own-lord-ACC laid-hand-on, saying, not indeed if-killing, own-lord-ACC laid-hand-on, saying, will-kill-(kü);
sentences.i: 'I have laid my hand on you, my own lord. If I do not kill you, they will say, "He laid hands on his own lord," and kill me;
sentences.n: This is the hardest passage of the part and my reading is a guess at the logic. I take Shirgügetü as saying: I have seized you, my own lord (qān(i)-jan γardaba, Ming 皇帝自的行 下手了, 'set hand to his own lord'); whether I kill you or not, I am a man who lifted a hand against his lord. ese teki alaγasu is 'not-indeed if-killing' (Ming 不曾 也 殺呵). The -kü ending (Ming 也) closes alaqu-kü, which I take as a statement of what will follow, 'they will kill'. (i)-jan is the accusative -i joined to the reflexive possessive -jan, 'his own'; the vowel written in brackets is the edition's.

sentences.t: alaγ̇asu teki mün-kü alaγdaqu-kü bi.
sentences.l: if-killing indeed so-(kü), to-be-killed-(kü) I.
sentences.i: and if I do kill you, I shall be killed all the same.'
sentences.n: The other branch of the same dilemma: alaγasu 'if killing', then mün-kü 'just so' (Ming 也), then alaγdaqu-kü, the passive of ala- (-γda-) with the future participle: 'will be killed'. bi is 'I'.

sentences.l: Only, at-least, at-own-dying, cushion taking, let-me-die
sentences.i: 'At least, in dying, let me take a cushion for my back and die!'
sentences.n: dere (Ming 墊背 'a pad for the back') is, I take it, the idiom for a companion carried into death: if he must die, he will take Tarqutai with him. That is an inference from the idiom, not from the Mongol. üküküi-dür(i)-jen: ükü- 'to die', the participle -küi, 'at' -dür, then the reflexive possessive -jen with a linking vowel. üküšü is a first-person optative, 'let me die' (Ming 死我). The quotation closes after this word and the narrative resumes.

sentences.l: Having said, astride-riding, big knife-with-own throat his cutting-through, at-reaching,
sentences.i: So saying, he sat astride him, and just as he reached with his own big knife to cut his throat through,
sentences.n: keġeġed is keġe- 'to say' with -ġed, the sequence converb ('having …ed'). quγulara (Ming 割折 'cut through') I take as quγula- with the converb -ra; kürküi-dür is kür- 'to reach' plus participle and -dür, Ming 到時 'at the arrival'. quγulara ... kürküi-dür is the moment of reaching in order to cut, before the cut is made, which is why Tarqutai can still cry out; what reaches what is not marked, and I take the knife reaching the throat. kituγai-jar-an is the instrumental -jar (here after the vowel -i; daγ̇u-γ̇ar in the next unit is the same ending after -u, so these two words do not show a rule for which form follows which sound) with -an, 'with his own'.

sentences.i: 'Shirgügetü is killing me! Once I am killed, what will you do, carrying off my dead body, with no life in it?
sentences.n: Tarqutai speaks. alan bijü is ala- 'to kill' with the converb -n and bijü 'is', a continuous 'is killing'; alan baraγasu is 'killing, if-finished' (bara-, the auxiliary of the earlier parts, 'once it is done'). ükügsen amin ügei beje min-u: 'my dead, life-less body' (the Ming glosses ükügsen 死了的). jakiγužai I read as ya- 'what' + ki- 'to do' with the future participle -γu and -žai; the ending -žai has no Ming gloss of its own and I take it as a question-marker, 'what will you do' (the Ming 做甚 gives only the question); the same ending is read 'lest' in ileġüžei below, where the Ming adds 恐, so the two readings are not shown to be one. ta 'you' (plural) is the subject, as the Ming 您 shows.

sentences.i: Before he can kill me, turn back, quickly!

'Turn back' here and below means to withdraw, not to go home.

sentences.i: Temüjin will not kill me.
sentences.n: Tarqutai explains why he is calm: he does not think Chinggis (still Temüjin to him) will have him killed. ülü with the future participle -qu is 'will not' (the ülü pattern: ülü goes with present or converb forms, ese with the past).

sentences.i: Of Temüjin, when he was small, I said, "There was fire in his eyes and light in his face";
sentences.n: The first of a run of 'saying' clauses (keġen), each one a thing Tarqutai told himself about the boy. γaltu and geretü are γal 'fire' and gere 'light' with -tü, 'having' (the possessive pattern: -tü as in 'wife-having'); the Ming reads them 火有的 and 光有的. nidün-dür(i)-jen and niγ̇ur-tur(i)-jan are 'in his own eye', 'in his own face': the locative, a joining vowel and the reflexive possessive. Temüžin-i has the accusative, 'of Temüjin', the one spoken about (the Ming 行); keġen then closes the clause. büleġe is the past 'was'.

sentences.i: "I will go and fetch him and bring him along; if I teach him, he will be like one who learns," I said;

sentences.i: Chinggis Qahan will say of us who came having laid hands on our own rightful lord:
sentences.n: The sentence begins again and takes the whole as a noun phrase: 'those who came, laying hand on their rightful lord'. iregsed is ire- with the plural participle -gsed. Here the reflexive is written tus(i)-jan, a variant of the same joint as above. The words that follow (unit 36) are what Chinggis is imagined to say; they speak of 'these' men and of 'us' (bidan-dur) as Chinggis would, so the 'us' of bidan-i here is Naya'a's own group seen from outside, in his report, and I do not write it into Chinggis's mouth.

sentences.i: "What reliable men are these? How should such men ever be comrades to us — men without any companions?
sentences.n: itegelten (Ming 中倚附的, 'leaning on, relying on') I read as 'having reliance', i.e. 'reliable', with -ten, which I read as a variant of the possessive -tü/-tai (uncertain; the Ming gives only 的). haran is 'people, common men', Ming 人. bidan-dur is 'to us' with the dative; nököčekün is nököče- 'to be a companion' and the future; nököčel ügeġün 'companion-less'. The sense I give: people with no loyalty of their own cannot be trusted as comrades. This is Naya'a's guess at how Chinggis would think, and it is a loose parse.

sentences.i: After that, Jaqagambu of the Kereid came to Chinggis Qahan to be his companion, when he was at Tersüd.
sentences.n: Teġün-ü qoina: 'after that' (qoina is a postposition, Ming 後). Žaqaγambu (Ming 人名) is the Kereid man; the Mongol does not say whose being at Tersüd büküi-dür 'when being' marks: Jaqagambu's or Chinggis's. I read it as Chinggis, but the order of the words fits either. nököčere: nököče- 'to be a comrade' with the converb -re (the Ming 做伴): 'as a comrade'.

sentences.i: There the ten thousand Tübegen, the many Tongqaid, and the Kereid people who had scattered all threw in their lot with Chinggis Qahan and came to him.
sentences.n: Three groups are named, in a row with no 'and': Tümen Tübegen (Ming 萬 姓, 'ten thousand' plus a clan name, parallel to olon Toṅγaid 'many Toṅγaid'; I take Tümen as the numeral, but it may be part of the name), olon Toṅγaid ('many Toṅγaid', Ming 多 姓(名)), and the Kereid people (irgen) who had 'scattered' (butaraγsan: butara- 'to scatter', the participle). ber (Ming 也) 'also, even'. orožu: oro- 'to enter', so 'having entered (his service)'. ireġüleġei: the stem looks like ire- with the causative -ġül-, but the Ming 來了來 reads it as plain 'came'; I follow the Ming and note it.

sentences.l: Kereid's Waṅ-Qaγan being, formerly, Jesügei Qaγ̇an's time, well peace living-together-at, Jesügei Qān-with anda had-spoken-together was.
sentences.i: As for Wang Qahan of the Kereid: in the days of Yesügei Qahan, while they lived together in peace and good will, he had sworn anda, sworn brotherhood, with Yesügei Qan.
sentences.n: A background sentence. bürün: bü- 'to be' with the time converb -rün, used as a topic marker, 'as for', and the Ming reads 有呵. Waṅ-Qaγan is the title of the Kereid ruler: a Chinese 王 'prince' joined to the Mongol qaγan; so in the English a plain 'Wang Qahan'. alduγsan-dur (Ming 共住, 'living together') I cannot analyse with certainty; I take it as a verb 'to live together' with the past participle and -dur. anda is the sworn brother, Ming 契合. keġeldügsen ažuγ̇u: keġe- with the reciprocal -ldü- and the past participle, then ažuγ̇u 'was': 'had agreed together'. Sai-bar el: sai 'good', -bar the instrumental, el 'peace, a realm in order' (Ming 治平). Yesügei is Qaγ̇an-u the first time and Qān-luγ̇a the second; I follow the printed forms (Qahan, then Qan) and take one man.

sentences.n: anda keġeldüküi is 'the anda (they) agreed together', and josun (Ming 理 'principle, what is right') is 'custom, rule'. The 'his' (in-ü) points to the anda-bond; I cannot say how the clause attaches until the verb, which is beyond the end of this part.

sentences.i: and because Wang Qan had killed the younger brothers of his own father, Qurchaqus-Buiruq Qan,
sentences.n: alaqu-jin tula: ala- 'to kill' with the participle -qu and the genitive -jin, then tula 'on account of' (Ming 上頭 'on top of'): 'on account of the killing'. Who killed whom I read from the Ming: Wang Qan killed the younger brothers of his father Qurchaqus-Buiruq (ečige-jüġen: ečige 'father' with the reflexive -jüġen, 'his own father'; qān-u deġü-ner(i)-jen 'the Qan's younger brothers'). This reading is uncertain; the genitives could also make the brothers Wang Qan's own. The next unit says Gür Qan rose, which fits the first reading.

sentences.i: Gür Qan, with his own uncle, rebelled and joined forces and massed at the Hara'un Narrows,
sentences.n: Gür is a name (Ming 人名), and with Qān it reads as a ruler's title. abaγa is 'paternal uncle', Ming 叔叔; -luγ̇a 'together with', -ban 'his own'. bulγa (Ming 反) is 'revolt'; bolulčažu is bolulča- 'to join together' (Ming 相從着, 'following one another'), and the same verb ends this passage. Haraγ̇un Qabčal: a mountain or defile (Ming 山名 on the first, 窄狹 'narrow' on the second); I treat it as one place 'the Narrows of Hara'un', which is a guess. širγuγ̇ulažu (Ming 共攢着 'crowding together') I cannot analyse.

sentences.l: Jesügei Qān him-ACC to-own being-come-to, own army mounting,
sentences.i: Yesügei Qan, to whom he had come, mounted his own army
sentences.n: This unit is the shakiest. iregdežü is ire- 'to come' with the passive -gde-, 'being come to' (Ming 被來着). ima-ji (Ming 他行) is the accusative of 'he'; it should mark the one who came, but the passive should make Yesügei the one come to. öġesün (Ming 自己的) 'his own', čerig 'army'. I read Yesügei, visited by Wang Qan, mounting his troops: 'Yesügei Qan, to whom he had come, mounted his own army'. The unit runs on into the next.

sentences.n: The part ends in the middle of a sentence: the Shiratori text breaks off at tere 'that' and the verb follows after the end of §150. in-ü ('his') I read as Gür Qan's, the people he lost. irge (Ming 百姓) 'people', orγa (人烟 'smoke of dwellings') 'households'. ögügšen-ü tula: ögü- 'to give' with the past participle and the genitive, 'on account of having given'. bolulčaqu: bolulča- 'to join together' as above, with the participle -qu, Ming 共做了的 'made together'.
